# Experiment results (auto-generated)

Regenerated by `python experiments/run_all.py`. Do not edit by hand.
Every number comes from synthetic data with fixed seeds — not a single line of production data is included.



---

## e1 · Consensus gate and review budget

Hypothesis — Can the degree of vote disagreement alone pre-sort label quality?

Labeling LLM called 5 times. Grades are assigned from the vote distribution alone — the oracle is used only for scoring.

| Grade | Rows | Share | Primary accuracy | Mean ambiguity |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| agree | 8771 | 0.439 | 0.9723 | 0.1316 |
| partial | 9555 | 0.478 | 0.7168 | 0.3750 |
| review | 1654 | 0.083 | 0.2703 | 0.4766 |

Unanimous band 0.972 vs split-vote band 0.270 — a 70.2pp gap. Even without converting vote counts into probabilities, using them only as a routing gate separates quality this much.

Spending the review budget in gate order vs at random (assuming reviewed rows are replaced with the true label):

| Review share | Before review | Gate first | Random | Δ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 5% | 0.7920 | 0.8282 | 0.8025 | 0.0257 |
| 10% | 0.7920 | 0.8592 | 0.8132 | 0.0460 |
| 20% | 0.7920 | 0.8994 | 0.8346 | 0.0648 |
| 40% | 0.7920 | 0.9595 | 0.8772 | 0.0823 |

H1b — call one more cheap model and keep only rows where 'the two agree'. A fair comparison is against the same-model repeated-call gate at the same coverage.

| Filter | Rows kept | Coverage | Primary accuracy |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Main LLM alone | 19980 | 1.0000 | 0.7920 |
| Cheap LLM alone | 19980 | 1.0000 | 0.4445 |
| Keep only rows where both models agree | 10720 | 0.5365 | 0.7840 |
| Main LLM unanimous rows only | 8771 | 0.4390 | 0.9723 |

Rows where the two models agree but both are wrong: 11.6%. The cheap LLM does not independently catch the main LLM's errors, but it does succeed at rejecting answers the main LLM got right — among rows dropped by the agreement filter, the share the main LLM had right is 0.801.

H1c — now LLM-as-a-judge. Instead of having the cheap LLM choose a new label, we only ask 'is this label correct?' and keep the accepted rows. A fair comparison with the gate requires matching coverage.

| Filter | Rows kept | Coverage | Primary accuracy |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Judge-accepted only (strictness=0) | 11691 | 0.5851 | 0.7936 |
| Judge-accepted only (strictness=1) | 7747 | 0.3877 | 0.8003 |
| Judge-accepted only (strictness=2) | 4315 | 0.2160 | 0.8090 |
| (Reference) same coverage 59% taken in gate order | 11691 | 0.5851 | 0.9351 |

At the same 59% coverage, the judge's accepted rows reach 0.794 while selecting in gate order gives 0.935. No matter how strict the judge is made, accuracy of the accepted rows stalls around 0.809 (at 22% coverage). The reason is simple — the judge gets confused in the same places as the labeling LLM. If it shares both the tendency to push items into the catch-all class and the tendency to pick one side of a confusable pair, the judge adds no information about those errors. For a judge to be worth its cost, it has to base its decision on something different from the labeling LLM.

Verdict — ✅ Supported. H1 supported. Grade alone separates quality by 70.2pp, and under the same review budget, gate-first beats random.

Verdict — ❌ Rejected. H1b rejected. Cross-model consensus loses a lot of coverage, and its accuracy gain is smaller than the same-model repeated-call gate. Adding the cheap LLM to the consensus also rejects answers the main LLM got right.

Verdict — ❌ Rejected. H1c rejected. At the same 59% coverage, LLM-as-a-judge accepted rows 0.794 < gate 0.935; even the strictest judge reaches only 0.809 (at 22% coverage). What matters is not attaching a judge per se but what the judge looks at. A judge that shares the same bias only adds call cost.

## e2 · A circular scorecard flips the ranking

Hypothesis — Scoring with labeling-LLM pseudo-labels / with an outside-the-pipeline signal / with the true labels — do the three give the same ranking?

Six small models. Architecture and hyperparameters are identical; only the training labels differ. The outside-signal score is measured only on rows where that axis distinguishes the top two candidates (axis 'routing-target assignment', 7 groups, observation noise 25%).

| Small model (training labels) | ① Pseudo-label eval set | ② Outside signal | ③ True labels | Pseudo EM | True EM |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 call | 0.8279 | 0.6542 | 0.7888 | 0.6906 | 0.6514 |
| 3 calls | 0.8285 | 0.6452 | 0.7661 | 0.6934 | 0.6509 |
| 5 calls | 0.8303 | 0.6507 | 0.7796 | 0.6990 | 0.6597 |
| 7 calls | 0.8287 | 0.6515 | 0.7806 | 0.7021 | 0.6671 |
| 5 calls + outside-signal fix | 0.8260 | 0.6663 | 0.8045 | 0.6945 | 0.6877 |
| 7 calls + outside-signal fix | 0.8238 | 0.6708 | 0.8124 | 0.6965 | 0.6992 |

Extracting only the rankings (leftmost is first):

| Scorecard | Ranking produced | Rank correlation τ with the truth |
|---|---:|---:|
| ① Eval set built from pseudo-labels (same source) | 5 calls > 7 calls > 3 calls > 1 call > 5 calls + outside-signal fix > 7 calls + outside-signal fix | -0.7333 |
| ② Signal from outside the pipeline | 7 calls + outside-signal fix > 5 calls + outside-signal fix > 1 call > 7 calls > 5 calls > 3 calls | 1.0000 |
| ②' Outside signal contaminated with the same bias | 7 calls + outside-signal fix > 5 calls + outside-signal fix > 3 calls > 5 calls > 1 call > 7 calls | 0.3333 |
| ③ Truth (oracle) | 7 calls + outside-signal fix > 5 calls + outside-signal fix > 1 call > 7 calls > 5 calls > 3 calls | 1.0000 |

②' is an axis that comes from outside the pipeline but is biased in the same direction as the labeling LLM (35% of observations are pulled toward the group the labeling LLM favors — the situation where the labeling LLM has also learned an operational auto-routing rule). τ drops from 1.00 to 0.33. Coming from an outside source is not sufficient on its own; one must also check that it is independent of the labeling LLM's bias. This is why, when the routing axis was used in practice, it had to be re-tested with the auto-routed items removed.

The pseudo-label eval set picks 5 calls as first; the true first is 7 calls + outside-signal fix. Choosing a model by this eval set alone leaves 3.28pp on the table against the truth. The outside signal's absolute score is low at 0.671 — because the axis is inherently coarse — but its ranking is right. Do not report its absolute score; use it only for relative comparison. Caveat: the ① scores of the models without the fix are very close (0.8279–0.8303), and there are only 6 models and a single seed, so each τ carries uncertainty.

Increasing the strength of the labeling LLM's systematic bias from 0, we re-measure the rank correlation of both scorecards. With bias 0 the pseudo-label eval set does not reverse the ranking (τ = +0.33, weakly positive) — the reversal appears only when there is bias. (Real LLMs are unlikely to have bias 0.)

| Bias β | ① Pseudo-label eval set τ | ② Outside signal τ | Mean true top1 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 0.0000 | 0.3333 | 1.0000 | 0.8715 |
| 0.4000 | -0.3333 | 1.0000 | 0.8535 |
| 0.8000 | -1.0000 | 1.0000 | 0.8206 |
| 1.1000 | -1.0000 | 1.0000 | 0.7911 |
| 1.6000 | -1.0000 | 1.0000 | 0.7443 |

Verdict — ✅ Supported. H2 supported. Rank correlation of the pseudo-label eval set τ=-0.73, outside signal τ=1.00. The model ranked first by labeling-LLM pseudo-labels was not first against the truth. A coarse axis with low absolute scores is a better scorecard than a circular axis with high absolute scores.

## e3 · Vote distribution as soft targets (KD)

Hypothesis — Does training on the vote distribution instead of the labeling LLM's final label improve the small model?

A single set of pseudo-labels from 5 labeling-LLM calls is trained in three target forms only. Data, architecture, and number of steps are all identical.

| Training target | True top1 | True EM | True multi-row EM | Circular top1 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| A hard (primary one-hot) | 0.7704 | 0.6555 | 0.0645 | 0.8287 |
| B set (primary .75 / secondary .25) | 0.7796 | 0.6597 | 0.0894 | 0.8303 |
| C soft (raw vote distribution) | 0.7899 | 0.6468 | 0.1753 | 0.8310 |

The first thing that stands out is that soft targets lower overall EM (B 0.6597 → C 0.6468), even though top1 and multi-row EM went up in the same table. Soft targets leave mass on the runner-up label, so top-2 is opened more often, and overall EM loses when multi-label predictions increase (→ the Pareto front in e5). This is the first place where 'better/worse' depends on the metric.

Where did true top1 move when switching from B (set) to C (soft)? Stratification uses only the labeling LLM's votes on the test side — stratification must be possible without the oracle to transfer directly to production.

| Stratum | n | B set | C soft | Δ(pp) | McNemar p |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Unanimous stratum (agree) | 8771 | 0.9566 | 0.9593 | 0.2736 | 0.0009 |
| Split-vote stratum (partial+review) | 11209 | 0.6412 | 0.6574 | 1.6237 | 0.0000 |
| All | 19980 | 0.7796 | 0.7899 | 1.0310 | 0.0000 |

Overall gain +1.03pp, split-vote stratum +1.62pp. The direction is as predicted — the gain comes only where the labeling LLM wavered. But the absolute size of the overall gain is small, so it hardly justifies the cost of retraining on its own. The real value of soft targets lies not in the score but in the fact that preserving the vote distribution makes post-hoc experiments like this possible without re-querying the LLM.

Verdict — △ Partially supported. H3 partially supported. The direction and location of the gain match the hypothesis (split stratum +1.62pp), but the overall +1.03pp is not large. Adopt it, but do not claim 'this is what delivers the performance'.

## e4 · Same LLM call budget, different allocations

Hypothesis — Should 90,000 calls be spent 'shallow and wide' or 'deep on split rows'?

Training pool 30,000 rows, budget 90,000 calls. The four left columns are the quality of the pseudo-labels themselves; the two right columns are the true-label scores of the small model trained on those pseudo-labels.

| Allocation | Calls spent | Rows labeled | Pseudo-label top1 | Pseudo-label EM | Multi rate | Small model true top1 | Small model true EM |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 3 calls × 30,000 rows | 90000 | 30000 | 0.7711 | 0.7148 | 0.0000 | 0.7650 | 0.6490 |
| 5 calls × 18,000 rows | 90000 | 18000 | 0.7874 | 0.6737 | 0.2059 | 0.7816 | 0.6611 |
| 7 calls × 12,857 rows | 89999 | 12857 | 0.8026 | 0.7175 | 0.1085 | 0.7805 | 0.6668 |
| 3 calls + 4 on split rows × 18,886 rows | 89994 | 18886 | 0.8013 | 0.7177 | 0.1004 | 0.7831 | 0.6668 |

The winning allocation is 3 calls + 4 on split rows × 18,886 rows. Versus 3 votes on every row: true top1 +1.81pp / EM +1.78pp. It actually labels fewer rows — meaning that fixing the labels of rows already paid for was cheaper than buying more rows.

Fixing the number of rows and increasing only the number of calls (ignoring the budget):

| Calls | Pseudo-label top1 | Pseudo-label EM | Pseudo-label multi rate | Unanimous share |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 0.7284 | 0.6725 | 0.0000 | 1.0000 |
| 3 | 0.7711 | 0.7148 | 0.0000 | 0.5570 |
| 5 | 0.7871 | 0.6714 | 0.2065 | 0.4377 |
| 7 | 0.8025 | 0.7151 | 0.1109 | 0.3787 |

Label selection (top1) improves monotonically with more votes, but exact match fluctuates — because the multi rate overshoots the true rate (0.113) and then comes back. In other words, 'how many votes to use' touches two problems at once: label selection and label count. Choosing the number of calls by exact match alone makes the two effects cancel out, so nothing is visible (→ e5).

Verdict — ✅ Supported. H4 supported. Under the same budget, targeted re-voting won (3 calls + 4 on split rows × 18,886 rows). But the gain comes not from 'spending many votes' but from 'not spending votes on unanimous rows'. Without the gate (e1), this allocation is not possible at all.

## e5 · The count problem: same experiment, conclusion flips with the metric

Hypothesis — Does a model that predicts the label count separately beat the one-line probability ratio?

The small model is fixed to a single model trained on pseudo-labels from 7 calls; only decoding changes. The count predictor was trained with the pseudo-label count as its target (no oracle used; accuracy against the true count 0.885).

The three scorers are compared at the same predicted multi rate (0.113, matched to the pseudo-label multi rate). Thresholds are set on val only; test is used only for reporting.

| Scorer (matched operating point) | t(val) | Overall EM(test) | Multi-row EM(test) | Predicted multi rate |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Probability ratio p2/p1 | 0.6155 | 0.6861 | 0.0536 | 0.1218 |
| Count predictor P(multi) | 0.1636 | 0.6883 | 0.1810 | 0.1120 |
| Combined P(multi)×(p2/p1) | 0.0734 | 0.6924 | 0.0746 | 0.1192 |
| (Reference) never predict multi-label | - | 0.7279 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 |
| Count given (upper bound) | - | 0.7836 | 0.4854 | 0.1148 |

At the same multi rate, overall EM is probability ratio 0.6861 vs count predictor 0.6883 (McNemar p=0.376) — any difference is in the third decimal place. Yet multi-row EM widens more than 3x, 0.0536 → 0.1810 (p=6.2e-42). The predictor knows something about 'which rows are multi-label' that the probability ratio does not — in this world, whether a row is multi-label depends on whether the two candidates form an allowed co-occurring pair, and that information is not contained in the ratio of the top two probabilities. Why overall EM still does not move is simple: multi-label rows are only 11.5% of the total, so the averaged metric swallows the gain entirely.

> Caution: this is where the lab diverges from the real pipeline. In production, when count predictors with the same structure were trained in several variants, none ever beat the probability-ratio gate. In the synthetic world the 'count' is determined by a clean rule (allowed co-occurring pairs), so the predictor has more to learn than in reality. → This is a point where a synthetic experiment cannot replace a production conclusion; a synthetic experiment is useful only when you can explain why the results differ.

Pareto front observed directly on test while sweeping the probability-ratio threshold:

| t | Overall EM | Multi-row EM | Predicted multi rate |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 0.1000 | 0.5063 | 0.3223 | 0.4911 |
| 0.2000 | 0.5781 | 0.2229 | 0.3671 |
| 0.3000 | 0.6209 | 0.1627 | 0.2828 |
| 0.4000 | 0.6453 | 0.1143 | 0.2229 |
| 0.5000 | 0.6671 | 0.0785 | 0.1702 |
| 0.7000 | 0.6974 | 0.0397 | 0.0910 |
| 0.9000 | 0.7182 | 0.0100 | 0.0285 |

Overall EM peaks at 0.7279 at t=1.00, where multi-row EM is 0.0000. Multi-row EM peaks at 0.3223 at t=0.10, where overall EM drops to 0.5063. No single t maximizes both axes at once. So t is not 'a value obtained by tuning' but an operational decision about which kind of error to accept.

Verdict — △ Partially supported. H5a partially supported — a case where the conclusion flips depending on what is measured. Overall EM shows no difference (0.6861 → 0.6883), while multi-row EM clearly supports it (0.0536 → 0.1810, p=6.2e-42). Had we reported overall EM alone and written 'count predictor rejected', we would have discarded a real signal because of metric design.

Verdict — ❌ Rejected. H5b rejected. The threshold that is optimal for overall EM differs from the one optimal for multi-label rows, and maximizing overall EM alone converges to 'never predict multi-label' (0.7279). That is, t is not a value obtained by tuning but an operational decision about which kind of error to accept. The upper bound when the count is given, 0.7836, shows the remaining headroom.
